questions.q: Which question does a plot, as opposed to a story, make the audience ask?
questions.explain: A story makes us ask 'and then?'; a plot, with its emphasis on causality, makes us ask 'why?'

questions.q: A character in a draft does something unexpected that, on reflection, fits perfectly. What would Forster say?
choices: It's a sign of a round character: surprising in a convincing way
It's a satellite and can be cut
questions.explain: Forster's test of roundness is the capacity to surprise convincingly.

questions.q: What is Forster's attitude to flat characters?
choices: They should be given a bone structure
They're useful: easy to recognize and remember, and Dickens is full of them
questions.explain: Forster defends flat characters, citing Dickens and Mrs Micawber.

questions.q: 'The queen died, no one knew why, until it was discovered that it was through grief.' What does this add to the basic plot?
choices: A mystery: the cause is withheld, then revealed
questions.explain: Forster says mystery, holding the reason back, is essential to plot at a higher level.

questions.q: What does Forster mean by 'bouncing' the reader?
choices: The novelist's power to carry the reader into accepting what's said, which matters more than consistent point of view
questions.explain: Forster thought shifts of viewpoint don't matter if the writer can carry the reader along.

questions.q: Which figure does Forster use to show the power of pure story?
questions.explain: Scheherazade survives by making the Sultan want to know what happens next.

questions.q: What does Forster mean by 'rhythm' in a novel?
choices: The alternation of scene and summary
A recurring image or phrase that returns with variations and gathers meaning
questions.explain: His model is the little phrase that recurs in Proust: repetition plus variation.

ideas: The test of a fully realized character is whether it can surprise us in a convincing way.
Some characters are built around a single idea or quality, and that makes them easy to remember, not worse.
Telling a story is a low, primitive pleasure, but no novel can do without it.
A novelist's power to carry the reader along matters more than keeping a consistent point of view.
